back: Testing done at every point in development to confirm that individual modules, or the whole solution, satisfy every requirement and work as intended. It takes place in an environment set up for development or testing, and can be done by the developers themselves, independent testers or high-level users.
mistake: Alpha testing isn't only programmers checking their own code: independent testers and high-level users can do it too. Beta testing differs in that intended user groups take part, and it also checks stability and usability on hardware like the target's.

back: Moving data that is rarely needed any more out of a working system and into storage that is accessed less often, where it is kept for possible later use or because rules require it to be kept. Held apart from the system for the long term, the data no longer adds to the system's storage load or slows its performance.
mistake: Archiving isn't the same as a backup. A backup is an extra copy kept in case the original is lost; archiving moves the data itself out of the working system so it stops taking up space there.

back: Copying data and keeping the copy apart from the original, so it can be restored if the data is lost. A copy can be full (everything), differential (changes since the last full copy), incremental (changes since the last copy of any kind) or a mix of these. Copies are made manually or automatically on a schedule, and kept on a separate local drive, on external storage or in the cloud.
mistake: Differential and incremental are easily swapped: differential counts from the last full backup, incremental from the last backup of any kind. Version control isn't a backup method either; the 2025 examiners' report called that an error.

back: Testing in which intended user groups try a solution, to check that it meets every requirement, works as expected, is stable and is usable by them. The environment can be for development, testing or production, but the hardware is the same as (or close to) what users will run it on. What testers report can lead to suggested or actual changes to modules or the solution.
mistake: Beta testers aren't hunting bugs or checking output values: they are intended users working through realistic scenarios while their behaviour is observed and recorded. The 2025 report gave no marks for saying participants would do bug testing or check the values a report outputs.

back: Recognising where computation applies to a problem and reasoning about it in logical, algorithmic, recursive and inferential ways. It usually draws on decomposition (breaking a problem into smaller parts), pattern recognition, abstraction, modelling and algorithms, which together can be used to build digital solutions.

The code structures that determine how a solution's algorithm behaves. Sequence: lines run one after another, in the order written. Selection (branching): a condition tested against the data decides which code runs (IF, IF…ELSE, IF…ELSEIF, SWITCH/CASE). Repetition (iteration): a condition makes code run again and again: pre-test (WHILE), post-test (DO…WHILE, REPEAT…UNTIL), or a set number of times decided by the context and data (FOR).
mistake: An IF…ELSEIF chain is selection: it picks one path. It isn't repetition (a loop runs a block again) or a method (not a control structure at all); over a quarter of students chose one of those on the 2025 exam.

back: Generally agreed approaches to using digital systems or representing data, followed so that a solution stays consistent throughout: for example, aligning data the same way in spreadsheet cells, or keeping a chart's axis scale consistent. Some are enforced (a password must contain certain characters); others are only recommended (giving an email a subject line).

Using a variety of techniques to develop ideas and designs. This includes forming, analysing and judging the questions asked, the data used and the decisions made; students apply these strategies to manage how they work through a problem.

A broad field with many sides, bringing together digital systems, how organisations operate, the threats facing data and systems, legal and ethical issues, and managing risk. Its measures aim to protect systems and data from many kinds of threat.
mistake: Cyber security isn't only technical controls such as encryption: it also takes in organisational practice, law, ethics and risk management. In 2025, answers that described a security control when asked for a strategy to improve secure development (training, onboarding, a risk management plan) earned no marks.

back: The methods and software that let organisations collect or extract data in many forms, correct data that is wrong or incomplete, analyse it for patterns, trends and relationships, reach inferences about it, and present the findings visually so the conclusions are clear and unambiguous.

A way of describing how sound data is overall, judged by its accuracy, authenticity, correctness, reasonableness, relevance and timeliness. High-integrity data is dependable and trustworthy; data without it shouldn't feed calculations or be the basis for decisions.
mistake: Passing validation doesn't prove integrity: validation only checks that data is reasonable and complete, so a wrong but sensible value still gets through. Integrity also takes in accuracy, correctness, authenticity, relevance and timeliness.

back: Data that comes into a solution from an outside file or system, whether the solution fetches it or is given it. A source can be unstructured, such as a plain text (TXT) file, or structured, such as a delimited (CSV) file or an XML file.
mistake: A CSV file is plain text underneath, but it counts as structured because delimiters split each line into fields. The study design classes plain text (TXT) files as unstructured, and delimited and XML files as structured.

back: Using software to present analysed data graphically, typically as a combination of charts, histograms, graphs, maps and network diagrams that is both appealing and informative. They help users explore large amounts of data to spot patterns and relationships. The graphics may be static or dynamic, and may include virtual and augmented reality.

Part of developing a solution in a programming language: finding the errors already in the code, fixing them, then testing that the changes work correctly. It happens during development, as the code is being written. Techniques include breakpoints, statements that display values as the code runs, and commenting out code.

Measures that summarise a data set. They are grouped as measures of central tendency (average and median) and measures of variability and spread (maximum, minimum, range, frequency and standard deviation).

Recognised qualities that help a solution work well, be easy to use and look good. The study design groups them under functionality (interactivity, navigation), usability (ease of use, accessibility) and appearance (alignment, balance, contrast, image use, space, and text and table formatting).
mistake: Contrast is a design principle, not a UX characteristic: when users can't tell what a control does, the problem is affordance (a quarter of students mixed these up in 2025). Proximity, repetition and hierarchy aren't study design principles.

back: Using critical and creative thought to come up with and judge new ideas, then defining the preferred solution precisely enough to build it with a digital system. It depends on understanding users' needs and finding ways to beat existing solutions on efficiency or effectiveness. Divergent thinking supports creativity by generating a wide range of ideas; convergent thinking selects the preferred solution and produces accurate, logical plans and instructions for building it.
mistake: Divergent and convergent are easily swapped: divergent thinking spreads out into many possible ideas (brainstorming is an example), while convergent thinking narrows them to one preferred solution and its detailed plans.

back: The hardware, software and other elements, together with how they are interconnected, that are used to build digital solutions. Linked to one another, such systems form a network.

Graphical displays of complex information or data that users can explore interactively. Unlike a static visualisation or chart, the data shown can change, either when the user interacts with it or when live data is added.

How well a solution, design, data and information security strategy or development practice works, and how far it achieves what it was meant to do. For solutions and designs, measures include accessibility, accuracy, attractiveness, clarity, communication of message, completeness, maintainability, readability, relevance, timeliness and usability. For security strategies: confidentiality, integrity and availability. For development practices: the security controls in place, exposure to vulnerabilities and risks, and legal compliance.
mistake: Effective isn't the same as efficient: effectiveness is how well the result serves its purpose (fewer errors, clearer feedback), while efficiency is the time, cost and effort used to get there (a faster workflow, lower cost). The 2025 report expected a separate example of each.

back: The time, cost and effort it takes to achieve the intended results: the less it takes, the better. For a solution, measures include the cost of manipulating data and files, its functionality and how fast it processes. For a network, measures include productivity, processing time, running costs and how much is automated.
mistake: Efficiency examples are about time, cost and effort (a faster workflow, fewer steps, lower running costs); fewer errors or clearer output are effectiveness examples. Keep the two apart when an answer asks for both.

back: Turning data and information from plain text into a coded form, to keep it from being compromised. There are two methods. The symmetric method uses one key both to encrypt and to decrypt. The asymmetric method uses a public key to encrypt the data and information, and a matching private key to decrypt it.
mistake: To protect sensitive data an application stores, encrypt it. A cloud backup only guards against losing the data, and making users log in with multi-factor authentication doesn't secure what is already stored; encrypted data that is stolen can't be read without the key.

back: Problems that stop a program working as expected. They are classed as syntax (the language's rules aren't followed, so the code can't be compiled and executed), logic (the program runs but produces incorrect output, such as a wrong calculation or a condition evaluated wrongly) or run-time (something fails during execution, such as overflow, index out of range, type mismatch or divide by zero, crashing the program unless handled).
mistake: A syntax error is a broken language rule, such as a missing symbol, that stops the code compiling; dividing by zero isn't one. Dividing by zero crashes the program while it runs (run-time), and a wrong result without a crash is a logic error.

back: Situations that call moral standards, principles or expectations into question, and that can affect individuals, organisations or both. The ones the study design lists for software development are ineffective security practices, use of artificial intelligence during development, intellectual property and copyright issues.
mistake: Using AI to write code isn't unethical in itself. The issue is how it is used: for example, an organisation becoming too reliant on AI to write its code.

back: How data and information physically look when they are presented, for example as images, graphs, tables, text or web pages. Each one sets characteristics such as the presentation style or arrangement, and the shape and size.

A process of coming up with ideas and building on them, cycling from a first concept through to a developed design. Ideas may be captured as text, images and drawings, or spoken aloud. Tools for it include mood boards, brainstorming, mind maps, sketches and annotations.
mistake: Brainstorming and mind maps aren't the same tool. A brainstorm collects related ideas around a central theme without structure; a mind map is structured, with ideas branching further out from the first-level ideas.

back: The process of making sure each member of an organisation can reach only the data, modules and systems needed for their assigned duties. Done well, no one can get into data, modules or systems beyond what they need, staff receive administrator or other high-level privileges only when necessary, and the organisation's exposure to risk and security breaches is reduced.
mistake: In a development environment, IAM isn't about confidential user data, which wouldn't be held there. It protects the code and development data by authenticating each developer and restricting what they can access.

back: Guidelines written so that organisations and governments apply strategies that keep their data and information secure across networks, and uphold the highest ethical standards. Those relevant to this study are Australia's Artificial Intelligence (AI) Ethics Principles, the Essential Eight and the Information Security Manual (ISM).

A single visual that gives an overview of a topic or area of interest by bringing complex data or information together. Its visual elements are combined so a reader picks up patterns or trends at a glance, or sees information shown as data visualisations. Common features are complementary colour schemes, easy-to-read fonts, headings, multiple graphs, simple charts and statistics.

The main laws that people, businesses and government bodies must obey when they use intellectual property or collect and hold private data and information. For this study they are the Copyright Act 1968 (Cwlth), the Health Records Act 2001 (Vic), the Privacy Act 1988 (Cwlth), including the Privacy Amendment (Enhancing Privacy Protection) Act 2012 and the Privacy Amendment (Notifiable Data Breaches) Act 2017, and the Privacy and Data Protection Act 2014 (Vic).
mistake: Not every misuse of data breaches copyright. The Copyright Act is breached by copying or changing someone else's work, such as editing another author's code, without permission; storing personal information insecurely is a matter for the privacy Acts.

back: Guidelines that keep the names given to parts of a digital solution consistent while it is developed, including the names of programs, functions, interface controls, variables, tables and files. Consistent names make the solution and its code quicker and easier to read and understand. Hungarian notation, camel casing and snake casing are examples.
mistake: Picking any convention isn't enough: the point is consistency. A new name must follow the convention the design already uses, so if the existing names use camel casing (totalCost), a new one does too (taxRate, not tax_rate).

back: Data that researchers gather themselves, straight from its sources, for example through surveys, interviews or observations. It is raw: nobody has processed or summarised it yet.

A detailed proposal for how a project will be managed, taking its requirements and constraints into account. Its features include identifying tasks, sequencing them, allocating time, and setting out dependencies, milestones and the critical path. In this study it is carried out with Gantt charts, which are also used to monitor and document the project's progress.
mistake: A milestone isn't a task with a duration. It marks a point in time, such as the end of a stage of the problem-solving methodology (design finished, so development can begin), against which progress is checked.

back: English-like statements, written in order, that represent an algorithm for solving a problem. There is no single standard, but common conventions include START/BEGIN and FINISH/END to mark where a program starts and finishes, IF…ELSE and SELECT for decisions (selection), and REPEAT…UNTIL, WHILE…DO and FOR…NEXT for loops (repetition or iteration).
Data that someone other than the researcher has already collected, summarised or analysed. It may be large in volume and kept in repositories or data sets, and reports and articles can count as well.

Measures that help protect individuals, systems, networks, organisations, and data as it is collected, communicated and stored. A control can be hardware, software, physical equipment, a procedure or an electronic measure. For software development, the study design lists version control and code repositories, robust identity and access management, encryption, code review, regular updates and patches to software, and separated development, testing and production environments.
mistake: A control isn't a strategy. Asked for a strategy to improve secure development practice, give developer training, onboarding/induction or a risk management plan; describing controls such as encryption or code review earned no marks in 2025.

back: Anything that could compromise the security or integrity of data and information, whether it is held on a digital system or passing between systems: an action, a device or an event. Threats can be accidental (deleting or overwriting data, misdelivering information, damaging equipment unintentionally), deliberate (insider threats, unauthorised access, stealing data or physical devices, malware, denial of service attacks, social engineering) or events-based (natural disasters and environmental factors, power or network outages, hardware failures, data corruption).
mistake: A phishing email sent by outsiders isn't an insider threat, even if an employee clicks the link: that is social engineering. An insider threat comes from someone within the organisation, such as a developer whose change to the development environment makes its code and data public.

back: A document describing what a software solution is intended to do and the environment it will work in. It captures the main work of the analysis stage of the problem-solving methodology, and should describe the functional and non-functional requirements, constraints, scope, user characteristics and technical environments. It also includes analytical tools (context diagrams, data flow diagrams, use case diagrams) showing existing processes and systems.

An approach that looks at the whole picture when identifying and solving problems. It analyses how the components of each information system (data, processes, people and digital systems) interact and relate to one another, to work out how they influence the way the whole system functions. In Unit 4 it is applied when analysing and evaluating an organisation's software development security strategies and recommending improvements.

Taking into account how users perceive a digital system and how they react as they interact with it. Its characteristics are affordance, interoperability, security (authentication and data protection) and usability.
mistake: Contrast isn't a UX characteristic (it's a design principle), and neither is portability. Name one of the four: affordance, interoperability, security or usability; the 2025 report gave no marks for other qualities.

back: Checking, by hand or electronically, that data is reasonable and complete. It includes existence (presence) checks, which make sure a required field holds a value and isn't blank; type checks, which confirm data is of the expected type; and range checks, which make sure data falls within set limits. It can happen as data is input or after it has been stored.
mistake: Validation checks that data is reasonable and complete, not that it is accurate (that's verification). An age of 34 passes a range check even if the person is really 43.

back: Checking that data is accurate and consistent, from the moment it is acquired or entered and throughout its manipulation and analysis. Techniques include proofreading, comparing the data against other sources, and making sure any visualisation of the data matches what was acquired or collected.
mistake: Verification isn't validation. Validation checks that data is reasonable and complete (existence, type and range checks); verification checks that it is accurate and consistent, for example by proofreading it or comparing it with its source.
